name: Soleus
func: A broad, flat calf muscle lying under the gastrocnemius. It points the foot down and keeps you steady when standing, and squeezes leg veins to push blood back to the heart.

levels.kid:
Under your big calf muscle is another one, flat like a fish. It is called the **soleus**, named after the **sole fish** because of its shape.

It is a quiet worker. When you **stand still**, the soleus is gently working all the time to stop you from tipping forward. It also helps push you up on your toes and forward when you walk.

The soleus also **squeezes your leg veins** like a sponge, pushing blood back up to your heart. That is why some people call it your "second heart"!
levels.hs:
The **soleus** is a broad, flat muscle in the **superficial posterior compartment** of the leg, lying **deep to the gastrocnemius**. Part of it bulges out on each side below the gastrocnemius, which you can see in a lean, muscular calf.

Unlike gastrocnemius, it starts entirely **below the knee**: from the back of the **head and upper fibula**, the **soleal line** on the back of the **tibia**, and a fibrous arch between them called the **tendinous arch of soleus**. Its tendon joins the gastrocnemius tendon to form the **Achilles tendon**, inserting on the **calcaneus**.

Because it does not cross the knee, it **plantarflexes the ankle** with equal effectiveness whether the knee is bent or straight. It is especially important for **posture**: when you stand, your body's centre of gravity lies slightly in front of the ankle, so soleus works constantly to keep you from falling forward.

It is supplied by the **tibial nerve** (S1–S2). Blood vessels and the tibial nerve pass under its tendinous arch into the deep compartment. Beneath it lie the deep calf muscles (tibialis posterior and the long toe flexors).
levels.college:
**Attachments:** posterior surface of the head and upper quarter of the fibula, the soleal line and middle third of the medial border of the tibia, and the **tendinous arch** spanning the tibia and fibula. Insertion through the calcaneal tendon on the calcaneus. Soleus fibres contribute mainly to the deeper, medial part of the Achilles tendon.

**Tendinous arch:** the **popliteal artery** and **tibial nerve** pass deep to it, where the artery divides into the **anterior and posterior tibial arteries**. The posterior tibial artery then gives off the **fibular (peroneal) artery**.

**Fibre type:** soleus is one of the most **slow-twitch** muscles in the body, about 70–80% **type I** fibres in most adults (higher in endurance athletes). This suits it to continuous postural activity with high fatigue resistance.

**Venous sinuses:** soleus contains large, thin-walled **intramuscular venous sinuses**. When it contracts, they empty forcefully into the deep veins; when it relaxes, they refill. This **soleal pump** is the main engine of venous return from the lower limb and explains the ankle swelling that develops with long periods of sitting.

**Innervation:** the **tibial nerve (S1–S2)**, with branches from the popliteal fossa and below the arch. **Blood supply:** branches of the popliteal, posterior tibial and fibular arteries.

**Accessory soleus:** an extra muscle belly present in a small percentage of people, which may present as a soft-tissue mass at the ankle and is occasionally mistaken for a tumour.
levels.phd:
Soleus is the model muscle of **postural control** and motor neuron physiology. **Henneman's size principle**, that motor units are recruited from small to large, was developed partly from soleus and gastrocnemius recordings in the cat. Soleus motor neurons are small, have low thresholds and slow conduction velocity, and their motor units are fatigue-resistant **type S units**, in contrast to mixed gastrocnemius units.

During quiet standing, the body behaves like an **inverted pendulum** pivoting at the ankles. Soleus provides most of the ankle stiffness required to balance it, with small, intermittent bursts of activity rather than steady contraction. Research using ultrasound shows soleus fascicles often move paradoxically (shortening as the body sways forward) because the Achilles tendon is too compliant for the muscle to act as a simple spring, implying active neural control is required.

The soleus **H-reflex** (Hoffmann reflex) is the most widely used electrophysiological probe of human spinal circuits. Stimulating the tibial nerve activates Ia afferents, which excite soleus motor neurons; the H-reflex amplitude changes with posture, task and training, and it is modulated by presynaptic inhibition, reciprocal inhibition and descending pathways. H-reflex conditioning in humans and animals shows the spinal cord itself can "learn".

Exercise physiology research highlights soleus metabolism: a "**soleus push-up**" protocol (Hamilton and colleagues, 2022) showed sustained low-level soleus contraction raised local oxidative metabolism and improved blood glucose regulation after meals, because this oxidative muscle can work for hours without fatigue. Replication is ongoing.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** test plantarflexion with the **knee flexed** to minimise gastrocnemius contribution (e.g., single-leg calf raises with a bent knee). Compare calf girth for wasting. The **ankle reflex (S1)** involves soleus heavily.

**Deep vein thrombosis** often begins in the **soleal venous sinuses**, where blood pools during immobility (long flights, surgery, hospital bed rest). Calf swelling, pain and tenderness are features, though many DVTs are silent. Compression ultrasound is the main test. DVT can lead to **pulmonary embolism**. Prevention includes early mobilisation, calf exercises, compression and medication in high-risk patients.

**Soleus strains** are common in runners, particularly older endurance athletes, and present with gradual-onset deep calf pain worse with running, often with less dramatic onset than gastrocnemius tears. MRI or ultrasound shows the site; intramuscular tendon involvement may prolong recovery.

**Chronic venous insufficiency** results from failure of the calf muscle pump or valves, causing swelling, skin changes and leg ulcers near the medial ankle.

**Soleal sling syndrome** describes compression of the tibial nerve or popliteal vessels at the tendinous arch, causing calf pain and sometimes sole numbness.

**Equinus** contracture (tight calf) is tested with the **Silfverskiöld test**: if ankle dorsiflexion improves when the knee is bent, gastrocnemius is the tight muscle; if it does not, soleus is also tight. This guides whether surgeons lengthen only the gastrocnemius or the whole Achilles tendon.

The **soleus flap** is often used to cover open wounds over the middle third of the tibia.

keyPoints: Flat calf muscle deep to gastrocnemius; starts below the knee
Joins the Achilles tendon; plantarflexes regardless of knee angle
Soleal venous pump drives blood return; DVT often starts here
Silfverskiöld test separates gastrocnemius from soleus tightness

test.q: What is the main fibre type in the soleus?
test.explain: Soleus is roughly 70–80% type I, ideal for continuous postural work.
Branches arise in the popliteal fossa and below the tendinous arch.

test.q: Why does soleus plantarflex well even with the knee bent?
choices: It is supplied by two nerves
It does not cross the knee joint
test.explain: Starting below the knee, its length is unchanged by knee position.

test.q: Which condition often starts in the soleal venous sinuses?
test.explain: Pooling blood in immobile calf veins promotes clotting.

test.q: Which clinical test distinguishes gastrocnemius from soleus tightness?
test.explain: Bending the knee relaxes gastrocnemius; if dorsiflexion improves, gastrocnemius is the tight one.
